name: Compare two objects directly by length
description: Student can directly compare the length of two objects by lining them up at one end, and say which is longer or shorter.
exampleOfSuccess: Given two pencils, the student lines up their ends and says the red one is longer.
commonError: Student compares without lining up the ends, judging by where the tops finish regardless of the starting point.
checkpointTask: Give the student pairs of objects of similar length. Ask which is longer and watch whether they align the ends.

name: Compare two objects by mass
description: Student can compare the mass of two objects by hefting (holding one in each hand) or using a balance, and say which is heavier or lighter.
exampleOfSuccess: Holding a rock and a sponge, the student says the rock is heavier; checks with a balance and the heavier side goes down.
commonError: Student assumes the bigger object is always heavier, ignoring what a balance or hefting shows.
checkpointTask: Give the student pairs including a small-heavy and large-light object. Ask which is heavier and to check on a balance.

name: Compare the capacity of two containers
description: Student can compare which of two containers holds more by filling one and pouring into the other.
exampleOfSuccess: Filling a short wide cup and pouring it into a tall thin glass, the student sees it overflows and says the cup holds more.
commonError: Student judges by height alone, assuming the taller container always holds more.
checkpointTask: Give two containers of different shapes. Ask the student to find which holds more by pouring sand or water.

name: Compare two lengths indirectly
description: Student can compare the length of two objects that cannot be moved together, using a piece of string or a third object as a go-between.
exampleOfSuccess: To compare a doorway and a shelf, the student cuts string to the doorway width and carries it to the shelf to compare.
commonError: Student tries to remember the size rather than using the string, or stretches the string differently each time.
checkpointTask: Name two fixed objects in the room. Ask the student to compare their length using a piece of string.

name: Order three or more objects by an attribute
description: Student can order three or more objects from least to most by length, mass or capacity.
exampleOfSuccess: Given three ribbons, the student lines up their ends and arranges them shortest to longest.
commonError: Student orders by comparing only neighbouring pairs and misplaces one, or does not use a consistent starting point.
checkpointTask: Give the student three or four objects. Ask them to put them in order by length, then by mass.

name: Compare the duration of two events
description: Student can compare two events and say which takes longer.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says brushing teeth takes less time than eating lunch.
commonError: Student judges by how much they enjoy the event rather than how long it lasts.
checkpointTask: Name pairs of familiar events. Ask the student which one takes longer.

name: Explain the reasoning for a comparison
description: Student can explain how they know which object is longer, heavier or holds more, referring to the comparison they made.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says 'the blue ribbon is longer because when I lined them up at the same end, it stuck out past the red one'.
commonError: Student states the answer but cannot explain the comparison, or gives a reason unrelated to the measuring.
checkpointTask: After any comparison, ask the student to explain how they know, listening for reference to lining up, balancing or pouring.
reviewNotes: Serves the 'communicating reasoning' clause of the achievement standard, which is explicit in Y1-AS-03.

name: Measure length with units end-to-end
description: Student can measure the length of an object by laying informal units end to end along it and counting how many.
exampleOfSuccess: The student lays paperclips along a pencil with no gaps and counts 6 paperclips long.
commonError: Student counts the units incorrectly, or starts measuring partway along instead of at one end.
checkpointTask: Give the student an object and identical units (blocks or paperclips). Ask them to measure its length and say how many units.

name: Recognise units must be the same size
description: Student can recognise that the units used to measure must all be the same size for the count to be fair.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown a length measured with mixed big and small blocks, the student says it is not fair because the blocks are different sizes.
commonError: Student measures happily with a mix of unit sizes and does not see a problem.
checkpointTask: Show the student a length measured with mixed-size units. Ask whether that is a fair way to measure and why.

name: Lay units with no gaps or overlaps
description: Student can place units end to end with no gaps between them and no overlaps.
exampleOfSuccess: Measuring a book, the student places each block touching the next, with none on top of another and no spaces.
commonError: Student leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, giving a wrong count.
checkpointTask: Watch the student measure an object with units. Check whether they leave gaps or overlaps.

name: Compare two lengths by measuring
description: Student can compare the length of two objects by measuring each with copies of a unit and comparing the counts.
exampleOfSuccess: The student measures a crayon as 4 cubes and a marker as 7 cubes, and says the marker is longer.
commonError: Student measures each with a different unit and then compares the counts directly, which is not fair.
checkpointTask: Give the student two objects and one type of unit. Ask them to measure both and say which is longer.

name: Measure a distance with footsteps
description: Student can measure a longer distance using footsteps or another larger informal unit.
exampleOfSuccess: The student walks heel-to-toe across the room and counts 12 footsteps.
commonError: Student takes uneven steps or leaves gaps between footsteps, so the count is unreliable.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to measure the distance across the room in footsteps, walking heel to toe.

name: Explain why different units give different counts
description: Student can explain why measuring the same object with two different-sized units gives a different number of units.
exampleOfSuccess: Measuring a desk as 5 hand-spans but 9 cubes, the student explains the cubes are smaller so it takes more of them.
commonError: Student thinks the desk changed length, or that one of the measurements must be wrong.
checkpointTask: Have the student measure one object with two different units. Ask why the two numbers are different.
reviewNotes: From elaboration 1. Conceptual late IC: the inverse relationship between unit size and count.

name: Name and order units of time
description: Student can name familiar units of time (hour, day, week, month, year) and order them from shortest to longest.
exampleOfSuccess: The student lists hour, day, week, month, year and says an hour is shortest and a year is longest.
commonError: Student mixes up the order, for example saying a week is longer than a month.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to name the units of time they know and put them in order from shortest to longest.

name: Sequence familiar events in order
description: Student can put familiar events in the correct time order.
exampleOfSuccess: The student orders 'wake up, school, dinner, bed' correctly, or names the days of the week in order.
commonError: Student lists events without a clear order, or starts the days of the week from the wrong day inconsistently.
checkpointTask: Give the student a set of daily events on cards. Ask them to put them in the order they happen.

name: Show events on a timeline
description: Student can place events on a simple pictorial timeline to show their order over time.
exampleOfSuccess: On a timeline of a day, the student places breakfast before lunch and lunch before dinner.
commonError: Student places events by where there is space rather than by when they happen.
checkpointTask: Give the student a blank timeline and event pictures. Ask them to place the events in order.

name: Choose a sensible unit for a duration
description: Student can decide whether an event would take closer to an hour, a day, a week, a month or a year.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says a birthday party takes about an hour and growing taller takes about a year.
commonError: Student picks a unit that is far too short or long, such as saying a school day takes a week.
checkpointTask: Name several events. Ask the student whether each takes closer to an hour, a day, a week, a month or a year.

name: Compare the duration of two events using time units
description: Student can compare two events and say which takes longer, using familiar units of time.
exampleOfSuccess: The student says the school holidays last weeks but a lesson lasts about an hour, so the holidays are much longer.
commonError: Student compares using vague words only and cannot link the events to time units.
checkpointTask: Name two events of clearly different length. Ask the student which takes longer and to use time units to say so.
